warmup.q: Which of these compiles: fun <T> f(x: T) = x.length, fun <T> g(x: T) = x.hashCode(), or fun <T> h(x: T) { } called as h(null)?
options: Only f, because the callers will pass strings
None of them: an unbounded T can do nothing
warmup.why: With no bound, T can be any type, nullable ones included, so you may only use what Any? has: hashCode, toString, ==. length isn't on every type, and the compiler doesn't know your callers. h(null) compiles because T may be a nullable type. A bound is how you ask for more.

opening:
In the shop's storeroom, one box carries a sign: "fruit only". The sign shuts out the hammer and the till roll. In return, whoever unpacks the box knows something about every item in it: each one has a weight, so it can go straight on the scales.

In Generics from zero, T was a blank on a label that each caller fills in. Any caller, any type. That freedom has a price, and it surprises people. Inside a generic function, you can't ask a T for its length, even when every caller you have in mind passes a String.

The trap is to think the compiler knows your callers. It only knows the label. In this lesson, we'll find out what a plain T can do, and write signs that say "fruit only" and "can be compared". Then we'll ask for two things at once with where, and keep null out of the box with T : Any. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a storeroom box marked "fruit only". A bound is that sign on a type parameter. T : Fruit and T : Comparable<T> shut some callers out and let the body weigh and compare, where asks for two things at once, and T : Any keeps null out.

Now look in your own code for a generic class whose get returns V? to mean "not found", such as a Cache<K, V>. If V has no bound, a stored null and a missing entry look the same.

Next, we'll look hard at the word we've leaned on all lesson: subtype. If an apple is a fruit, is a crate of apples a crate of fruit?

sections.h: What a T with no bound can do: only what Any? can do
sections.html:
Start with a plain type parameter, one with no sign on it at all. It means "some type, I don't know which", so inside the function, T can do only what every type can do. In Java, the type that every object belongs to is Object. In Kotlin, "every type" includes the nullable ones, such as String?, so a T with no bound is held to Any?.

Java
static <T> String describe(T x) {
    return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + Objects.hashCode(x);
}

describe("Gala");   // fine
describe(180);      // fine
describe(null);     // fine: any Java T accepts null
Kotlin
fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}"

describe("Gala")    // fine
describe(180)       // fine
describe(null)      // also fine: T is inferred as Nothing?

toString(), hashCode() and == work, because they exist on Any?. The demo prints value=Gala, hash=2211823, value=180, hash=180 and value=null, hash=0. Anything more specific fails, even when every caller you have in mind would pass a String:

Java
static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); }
// error: cannot find symbol: method length()
Kotlin
fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length
// error: unresolved reference 'length'.

The compiler isn't being fussy. Someone could call lengthOf(42), and an Int has no length. A generic function must work for every type the caller is allowed to pick, so it can only use what all of them share.

Comparison fails the same way. Java says cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T). Kotlin gives a stranger message:

Java
static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }
// error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T)
Kotlin
fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b
// error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(other: String, ignoreCase: Boolean = ...): Int'
//        is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch.

In Kotlin, a > b means a.compareTo(b). The compiler goes looking for any compareTo it could use on a T, finds only the one on String, and reports that this one doesn't fit. It's a roundabout way of saying no. When an error mentions some unrelated type's method, read it as "this operation isn't defined for T".

The null case surprises people coming from Java, where every T accepts null anyway and nobody thinks about it. In Kotlin, fun <T> f(x: T) accepts null too, because T may be String? or Nothing?. (Nothing? is the type Kotlin gives a bare null. Write val x = null, then val y: Int = x, and the error says actual 'Nothing?'.) If your function must not see null, you have to say so. The last section shows how.

That is the job of a bound: a sign on the type parameter that promises more about T. The caller can pick from fewer types, and in return your code can do more with the one they pick.

sections.h: A box that only takes fruit: upper bounds
sections.html:
Here is the sign from the opening, written in code. The shop's fruit share an interface, Fruit, with a name and a weight in grams, and Apple is a small data class that implements it. An upper bound says "T must be this type or a subtype of it". For now, read subtype as a class that inherits from it, the way Apple inherits from Fruit; the next lesson gives the word its exact meaning. Java writes the bound with extends, even for interfaces. Kotlin writes it after a colon:

Java
interface Fruit { String name(); int grams(); }
record Apple(String name, int grams) implements Fruit {}

static <T extends Fruit> T heavier(T a, T b) {
    return a.grams() >= b.grams() ? a : b;      // grams() comes from the bound
}

Apple apple = heavier(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150));
Kotlin
interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int }
data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit

fun <T : Fruit> heavier(a: T, b: T): T =
    if (a.grams >= b.grams) a else b             // .grams comes from the bound

val apple: Apple = heavier(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))

The bound does two jobs. Inside the function, a.grams compiles, because every T is now some kind of Fruit. At each call, the sign turns everything else away: heavier("Gala", "Fuji") fails with argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Fruit' was expected.

You may wonder why heavier needs a T at all. Why not take two Fruit parameters and return a Fruit? Because then two apples in would give a Fruit out. To get your Apple back, you'd need a cast, the very thing lesson 1 of this track removed. With T, two apples in give an Apple out.

The most common bound in practice isn't a class you wrote. It's Comparable<T>:

Java
static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) {
    return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

maxOf2(180, 150);                                   // 180
maxOf2("Gala", "Fuji");                             // Gala
Kotlin
fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b

maxOf2(180, 150)                                    // 180
maxOf2("Gala", "Fuji")                              // Gala
maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30))   // 2026-11-02

Read T : Comparable<T> aloud as "T is something that can be compared with another T". Int is a Comparable<Int>, String is a Comparable<String>, and LocalDate, the JDK's class for a calendar date, is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>. Kotlin accepts that last one because Comparable is declared in T, which lesson 5 of this track explains. Inside the function, a > b now compiles, because the bound guarantees a compareTo.

The T appears twice in T : Comparable<T>, and that's on purpose. Comparable<T> says what T can be compared with. A bound that mentions its own type parameter is called a recursive bound. You'll meet it again in Enum<E : Enum<E>>, and in builder classes in lesson 10 of this track.

Now hand the comparing function two apples:

Java
maxOf2(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150));
// error: method maxOf2 ... cannot be applied to given types
//   reason: inference variable T has incompatible bounds
//     upper bounds: Comparable<T>   lower bounds: Apple
Kotlin
maxOf2(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))
// error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Apple',
//        but 'Comparable<uninferred T (of fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2)>' was expected.

Apple has no natural order. Should two apples compare by weight, by name or by price? The compiler won't guess, and it's right not to. Make Apple implement Comparable<Apple>, and the call compiles. Or, usually better, keep Apple plain and pass a Comparator where you need an order.

The sign picture breaks in one place. A real "fruit only" sign is checked by a person, who looks at the item. The compiler can only trust what the types declare. A class with a grams property that doesn't say : Fruit is still turned away.

One real difference between the languages shows up with LocalDate. In Java, LocalDate later = maxOf2(day1, day2) fails, because the strict bound forces T to be ChronoLocalDate. The JDK writes <T extends Comparable<? super T>> to fix that. Kotlin's plain T : Comparable<T> already returns a LocalDate.

A bound shuts some callers out and lets the body do more. Ask for exactly what the body uses.

One bound per type parameter covers most code. Sometimes, though, the body needs two abilities at once.

video.title: A plain T can only do what Any? does; an upper bound such as T : Fruit is a fruit-only sign that shuts some callers out and lets the body weigh and compare

sections.h: Two requirements at once: the where clause
sections.html:
A type parameter can have more than one bound. The angle brackets hold only one, so the rest go into a where clause after the signature. Java joins the bounds with &. Here is a function that picks the shortest name from a list, and uses alphabetical order to break a tie:

Java
static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortestLabel(List<T> items) {
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T item : items) {
        if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item;           // CharSequence gives length()
        else if (item.length() == best.length() && item.compareTo(best) < 0) best = item;
    }
    return best;
}
Kotlin
fun <T> shortestLabel(items: List<T>): T
        where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> {
    var best = items[0]
    for (item in items) {
        if (item.length < best.length) best = item     // CharSequence gives .length
        else if (item.length == best.length && item < best) best = item   // Comparable gives <
    }
    return best
}

T must meet every bound at once. A String is both a CharSequence, the JDK's interface for anything made of characters, and a Comparable<String>, so it fits. An Int is comparable but has no characters:

error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly.
error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'CharSequence' was expected.

You get two errors for one mistake. The first says the compiler gave up looking for a T. The second says why: an Int isn't a CharSequence, so no T can meet both bounds. When "cannot infer type" appears next to a mismatch, read the mismatch first. It's the real reason.

Here is one that surprises people: shortestLabel(listOf(StringBuilder("plum"), StringBuilder("lime"))) compiles. StringBuilder became a Comparable<StringBuilder> in JDK 11, so it sits in the overlap too.

At most one bound may be a class. The others must be interfaces, because a class can extend only one other class. Java also wants the class first:

Java
static <T extends Number & Exception> void numberOrError(T t) {}          // error: interface expected here
static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T clampToZero(T x) { ... }      // fine: class first
static <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> T wrong(T x) { ... }            // error: interface expected here
Kotlin
fun <T> numberOrError(t: T) where T : Number, T : Exception {}
// error: only one of the upper bounds can be a class.
fun <T> clampToZero(x: T): T where T : Number, T : Comparable<T> = x      // fine
fun <T> anyOrder(x: T): T where T : Comparable<T>, T : Number = x         // also fine

Kotlin has no ordering rule. It just counts classes.

The figure draws each bound as a fence around the types a caller may pick. Each new bound moves a fence in, and a where clause with two bounds leaves only the overlap.

Use where when the function needs two abilities that no single type in your code names. If you find yourself writing the same pair of bounds in five places, that pair probably wants to be one interface of your own.

So far, every bound has asked for more abilities. The last one asks for less: it takes null away.

sections.h: Keeping null out of the box: T : Any
sections.html:
The default bound is Any?, so T may be a nullable type. Most of the time that's what you want: a Box<String?> is a fine thing to have. Sometimes it quietly breaks your API, the functions and classes that other code calls. Here is a small cache that notes any problem found with each crate in the storeroom. The Java version has the same problem, because HashMap happily stores null values:

Java
class Cache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>();
    void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); }
    V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); }   // null means "no entry"... usually
}

Cache<String, String> problems = new Cache<>();
problems.put("apples", null);                   // "checked: no problem"
problems.get("apples");                         // null
problems.get("figs");                           // null, but never checked
Kotlin
class Cache<K, V> {
    private val entries = HashMap<K, V>()
    fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value }
    fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key]     // null means "no entry"... usually
}

val problems = Cache<String, String?>()
problems.put("apples", null)               // "checked: no problem"
problems.get("apples")                     // null
problems.get("figs")                       // null, but never checked

With V = String?, get returns null for two different reasons: "we checked the apples and found no problem", and "nobody ever checked the figs". The demo prints apples -> null and figs -> null, then its last line: Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller.

The fix is the bound T : Any, which means "any type, but not a nullable one". Java has no such bound, so the closest it gets is a check at run time:

Java
void put(K key, V value) {
    entries.put(key, Objects.requireNonNull(value, "no null values"));   // fails at run time
}
Kotlin
class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> { ... }

Cache<String, String?>()
// error: type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)'
//        must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'.

Now V? in get always means "absent", because a stored value can never be null. The same bound helps functions that must return a real value:

Java
@SafeVarargs
static <T> T coalesce(T... values) {
    for (T v : values) if (v != null) return v;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("all values were null");
}

String variety = coalesce(null, "Gala", "Fuji");   // the type says nothing about null
Kotlin
fun <T : Any> coalesce(vararg values: T?): T {
    for (v in values) if (v != null) return v
    throw IllegalArgumentException("all values were null")
}

val variety: String = coalesce(null, "Gala", "Fuji")   // String, not String?

The parameters are T? and the return type is T, and that difference only means something because T itself can't be nullable. Pass a bare null to a plain T : Any parameter, and you get null cannot be a value of a non-null type.

When null already has a job in your API, such as "not found", a nullable T gives it two. Write T : Any. Leave the default when holding a nullable value is fine, as in a Box<String?>.

Java types carry no nullability. A Java <T> always allows null. The best you can do is a run-time check, or an annotation such as @NonNull, which Kotlin reads when it calls the Java code. Lesson 10 of this track shows a related Kotlin tool, T & Any. It's for the rare case where one signature needs both a nullable T and a non-null version of it.

That's also where bounds stop. A bound says what one T may be. It says nothing about how two generic types relate to each other. Whether a crate of apples may stand in for a crate of fruit is a different question, and the next lesson's.

steps: Run NullBoundDemo (or NullBoundDemoJava). Look at the two lines it prints for apples and figs.

Change the Kotlin class header to class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> and run again. Java has no such bound: in the Java twin, uncomment the requireNonNull line instead, and see that it fails only when it runs.
Fix main so it compiles. How would you now record "checked: no problem"? (One answer: store an empty string. A better one: a small sealed interface CheckResult with a NoProblem object.)

Is that always true? */ class Cache<K, V> { private val entries = HashMap<K, V>() fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value } fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key] } fun main() { // V = String? is allowed, because the default bound of V is Any? val problems = Cache<String, String?>() problems.put("apples", null) // "we checked the apples: no problem" println("apples -> ${problems.get("apples")}") // stored null println("figs -> ${problems.get("figs")}") // never checked println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller.") }

alt.title: NullBoundDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l02.demo; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** Java twin of NullBoundDemo.kt. Java has no T : Any, so null stays ambiguous unless you check at run time. */ public class NullBoundDemoJava { static class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>(); void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); } // HashMap accepts null values V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); } // null: absent, or a stored null? } public static void main(String[] args) { Cache<String, String> problems = new Cache<>(); problems.put("apples", null); // "we checked the apples: no problem" System.out.println("apples -> " + problems.get("apples")); // stored null System.out.println("figs -> " + problems.get("figs")); // never checked System.out.println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller."); // Java's closest fix is a run-time check. Uncomment, run, and see where it fails. // Objects.requireNonNull(null, "stored values must not be null"); } }

try.expect: The first run prints apples -> null and figs -> null: a stored null and a missing entry look the same. With the bound, Cache<String, String?>() no longer compiles: Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. From then on, get returning null can only mean "not there". The Java twin's requireNonNull compiles and throws a NullPointerException with your message, but only when that line runs.

compare.title: Bounds in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Bounds.java
java.html: import java.util.List; class Bounds { // one bound: extends, even for an interface static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // two bounds with &: the class (if any) must come first static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortest(List<T> items) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item; } return best; } // no way to say "not null": T may always be null static <T> T firstOrThrow(List<T> items) { return items.get(0); // could be null } }

kotlin.title: Bounds.kt
kotlin.html: // one bound: a colon fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a >= b) a else b // two bounds: a where clause, in any order, at most one class fun <T> shortest(items: List<T>): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { var best = items[0] for (item in items) { if (item.length < best.length) best = item } return best } // T : Any rules out nullable type arguments fun <T : Any> firstOrThrow(items: List<T>): T = items[0] // never null

compare.note: The bounds mean the same thing in both languages and compile to the same JVM bounds. Kotlin uses a colon and a where clause and doesn't care about order. Java uses extends and & and wants the class first. The real difference is nullability. Kotlin's default bound is Any?, so you can opt out of null with T : Any. Java has no nullable types, so every Java T allows null, and only annotations can say otherwise. One small surprise: javap, the JDK tool that prints what a class file contains, shows Kotlin's T : Comparable<T> as <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T. Lesson 5 of this track explains that ? super.

worked.title: Build a size window that works for any comparable type

steps.say: The shop puts apples between 150 g and 250 g on the front shelf, and it runs a sale from 2 to 6 November. You want one class for both ranges: a window with a start and an end, both included. Start without a bound, and see what breaks.
steps.code: class Window<T>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { operator fun contains(value: T) = start <= value && value <= endInclusive // error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(...)' is inapplicable // because of a receiver type mismatch. }

alt.html: class Window<T> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; // error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T) } }

steps.say: 1. Ask for exactly the ability you use. The body only compares, so the bound is T : Comparable<T>. Now <= resolves to compareTo.
steps.code: class Window<T : Comparable<T>>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { init { require(start <= endInclusive) { "start $start is after end $endInclusive" } } operator fun contains(value: T): Boolean = start <= value && value <= endInclusive }

alt.html: class Window<T extends Comparable<? super T>> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { if (start.compareTo(endInclusive) > 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start is after end"); this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; } }

steps.say: 1. Use it with types that already fit the bound. Int and LocalDate are comparable out of the box. Self-check: why does Window(1, "z") fail? (Both values must be the same T. Kotlin settles on Int from the first one, then reports actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected.)
steps.code: val frontShelf = Window(150, 250) 180 in frontShelf // true val sale = Window(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)) LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4) in sale // true

alt.html: var frontShelf = new Window<>(150, 250); frontShelf.contains(180); // true var sale = new Window<>(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)); sale.contains(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4)); // true (needs the ? super T form for LocalDate)

steps.say: 1. Make your own type fit. A plain Int doesn't say what it measures. A Grams value with an explicit order does, and the window needs no change at all.
steps.code: data class Grams(val value: Int) : Comparable<Grams> { override fun compareTo(other: Grams): Int = value.compareTo(other.value) } val frontShelf = Window(Grams(150), Grams(250)) Grams(270) in frontShelf // false

alt.html: record Grams(int value) implements Comparable<Grams> { public int compareTo(Grams other) { return Integer.compare(value, other.value); } } var frontShelf = new Window<>(new Grams(150), new Grams(250)); frontShelf.contains(new Grams(270)); // false

lab.title: Bound your type parameters: maxOfAll, Window, shortestLabel, coalesce
steps: Run the tests once. All nine fail.
In Bounds.kt, write maxOfAll with a loop and >. Then try deleting : Comparable<T> from its signature to see the error, and put it back.
In Window.kt, add the require in init, then write contains, clamp and overlaps using only <, <=, > and >=. The tests use it for weights in grams, for days and for plain numbers.
Write shortestLabel. It uses .length from one bound and < from the other.
Write coalesce. Notice that the test assigns its result to a plain String.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: require(condition) { "message" } throws IllegalArgumentException when the condition is false.
Two windows do NOT overlap when one ends before the other starts: endInclusive < other.start || other.endInclusive < start. Negate that.
In coalesce, if (value != null) return value smart-casts value from T? to T.

drill.title: Write three bounded signatures from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write only the signatures (no bodies): (1) a function largest that returns the biggest item of a List<T> for any comparable T; (2) a function trimAndSort that takes a List<T> where T is both a CharSequence and comparable to itself; (3) a class Registry with a key type and a value type, neither of which may be nullable. Then write (1) and (2) in Java.

answer.html: fun <T : Comparable<T>> largest(items: List<T>): T = TODO() fun <T> trimAndSort(items: List<T>): List<T> where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> = TODO() class Registry<K : Any, V : Any> // Java: // static <T extends Comparable<T>> T largest(List<T> items) // static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> List<T> trimAndSort(List<T> items)

alt.title: Signatures.java
alt.html: static <T extends Comparable<T>> T largest(List<T> items) { ... } static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> List<T> trimAndSort(List<T> items) { ... } // Java has no non-null bound: the closest is a run-time check in the constructor or in put() class Registry<K, V> { void put(K key, V value) { Objects.requireNonNull(key); Objects.requireNonNull(value); } }

recap: An unbounded T has the bound Any?: you can use toString, hashCode and ==, and callers may pass null.
An upper bound such as T : Fruit or T : Comparable<T> shuts some callers out and lets the body use what the bound promises, such as .grams or <. Two apples in still give an Apple out.
More than one bound goes in a where clause. At most one bound can be a class. Java writes <T extends A & B> with the class first.
T : Any rules out nullable type arguments, so T? in your API can only mean "absent". Java type parameters always allow null.
The limit: a bound says what one T may be. It says nothing about whether a generic type of a subtype, such as a crate of apples, may stand in for a crate of fruit.

explain.prompt: In your own words: what does adding a bound to a type parameter take away from callers, and what does it give the function body? Use T : Comparable<T> and T : Any as your two examples.
explain.answer: A bound narrows the set of types a caller may pick. In exchange, the function body can rely on more. With no bound, T might be anything, including a nullable type, so the body can only use what Any? has. With T : Comparable<T>, callers can no longer pass types that have no order, like a plain Apple data class, but the body can now use < and >. With T : Any, callers can no longer pick a nullable type, but the body and the API get a guarantee: a T is never null, so a T? return can only mean "absent". In both cases the compiler enforces the deal at every call, like a sign on a box that turns the wrong items away.

deeper.html:
Why does javap show Kotlin's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) as <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2(T, T)? Because Kotlin declares Comparable<in T>, and when Kotlin writes a Java signature for a parameter of an in type, it adds ? super. That is also why Kotlin accepts LocalDate, which is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate> and not a Comparable<LocalDate>.

Java's own Collections.max shows how messy this gets without declaration-site variance:

Java
public static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> coll)
Kotlin
fun <T : Comparable<T>> Iterable<T>.max(): T

The Object & part is there for backward compatibility: it keeps the erased signature returning Object, as it did before Java 5. The ? super T lets a List<LocalDate> through. The ? extends T lets a collection of a subtype through. Kotlin's version gets the same flexibility from in and out, declared once on Comparable and Iterable. Lessons 4 to 6 of this track build up to reading that Java signature with ease.

One more bound rule: a type parameter bounded by another type parameter can't have extra bounds. fun <T, U> f(u: U) where U : T, U : Comparable<U> gives type parameter cannot have any other bounds if it's bounded by another type parameter.
